query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor molybdenum (≈2 at.%) to a standard CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy will trigger the in‐situ formation of a stable, nanolayered Mo oxide (MoO₃) at the sliding interface during wear, thereby maintaining a low coefficient of friction and reducing wear rate over the entire temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy matrix with typical phase stability and without self‐lubricating surface features.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a minor (~2 at.%) addition of Mo into the alloy composition by adjusting the feedstock during alloy fabrication.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted under controlled loads and environments with temperatures ramped continuously from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, adherent, nanolayered MoO₃ tribo‐oxide film at the sliding interface.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, the Mo dopant preferentially oxidizes to form MoO₃, a layered oxide with low shear strength that acts as a solid lubricant. This oxide film reduces interfacial shear stresses and prevents excessive material removal, and its formation is self-regulated by the operating temperature such that it is maintained both at room temperature and at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy—which typically exhibits rising friction coefficients and wear rates with increasing temperature—the Mo-doped alloy will show a significantly lower and more stable friction coefficient (e.g., reduced by over 20%) and a reduced wear rate (e.g., lowered by over 50%) across the tested temperature range.
generation.baseline: The base CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without Mo shows acceptable sliding behavior at room temperature but experiences increased friction and wear as temperature approaches 800 °C.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected under sliding conditions typical of laboratory tribological tests; however, effectiveness may be limited if the Mo content is too high (which could adversely affect the matrix properties) or under environmental conditions that disrupt the formation or stability of the protective MoO₃ layer (e.g., extremely oxidizing or reducing atmospheres beyond the test conditions).
generation.uncertainty: While MoO₃ is known to have lubricious characteristics, the optimal Mo concentration, thickness, adhesion, and long-term stability of the oxide film under cyclic loading and varying atmospheres remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one standard CoCrFeNi alloy (control) and one with a minor (~2 at.%) Mo addition. Using identical processing conditions, produce bulk samples and machine them into test coupons. Subject both sets to reciprocating sliding wear tests under identical controlled loads and environmental conditions, while gradually increasing the temperature from room temperature to 800 °C. Post-test, analyze friction data in real time, measure overall wear volumes, and characterize the worn surfaces via SEM and XPS/TEM to verify the presence and quality of any MoO₃ layers.
measurements: Real-time coefficient of friction versus temperature
Surface oxide phase identification using XPS and TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >20% lower friction coefficient and >50% lower wear rate) compared to the undoped control across the full temperature range, or if a MoO₃ tribo-oxide film is not observed on the worn surfaces, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
